newsitem.title: CHINA: China police detain dissident after open letter.
newsitem.headline: China police detain dissident after open letter.

text.p: Chinese police detained veteran dissident Jin Cheng overnight after he issued a daring call for a disgraced former Beijing leader to be brought to public justice, the activist's wife said on Friday.
Police took Jin from his home in western Beijing on Thursday evening and did not allow him to return until early on Friday, said the 38-year-old former official's wife, Liu Xiuli.

Jin on Tuesday sent an open letter to the head of China's National People's Congress, or parliament, calling for former Beijing Communist Party chief Chen Xitong to be punished for prompting a bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protests in 1989.
"The police took him away at 6.30 p.m. (1030 GMT) and he didn't come back until 2.00 a.m. (1800 GMT)," said Liu. "It was because of the open letter he sent."
Appeals and petitions to the communist-led government that touch on sensitive issues are a risky political act in China, which has clamped down hard on dissent in recent years.
The tough official reaction to his call for public justice had come as no surprise to the veteran activist, Liu said.
"(The detention) was just as he expected," said Liu. "This kind of thing has often happened in the past."

Jin was jailed for publishing an underground magazine in the period after the 1989 crackdown on student-led demonstrations in Beijing and has been the target of police surveillance and occasional detention since his release in 1993.

He said earlier this week that he was not afraid of the consequences of his call for public justice to be dealt to Chen, who has been out of the public eye since being toppled from his posts as Beijing party secretary and member of the elite party Politburo during a huge corruption scandal in 1995.
Beijing residents remained deeply concerned about the lack of a public accounting for Chen, whose name has become a byword for graft in the Chinese capital, he said.

Chen had also misrepresented the motives and goals of the demonstrators who filled the streets of the capital in 1989, prompting leaders to order the bloody army assault on June 4 that year, he wrote in his open letter.
Aside from his role in the crushing of the Tiananmen Square democracy demonstrations, Chen should be publicly tried for corruption and abuse of power, Jin said.

Whether to review the 1989 killing of hundreds of protesters remains one of the most sensitive issues facing China's leaders, who will in September or October hold a crucial congress to appoint leaders and fix policy for the next five years.

The death last February of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who publicly backed the crackdown, was widely seen as an opportunity for Beijing to alter its judgment that tough action was needed in 1989 to end a counter-revolutionary rebellion.
However, analysts have said top leaders are unlikely to rethink their stand on the crackdown in the near future, despite calls from dissidents and private pressure from some officials.
